summary: Most reviewers find the Skwama a comfortable, versatile all-rounder, praised for its roomy toe box and good heel hooks. The main downside is wear, with heel seams tearing and soft rubber needing a resole within months for many. Painful heel and Achilles rubbing, and a rough break-in when sized down hard, come up too. Suits wide feet well.

Most reviewers use the Instinct VSR as a versatile all-rounder with good edging and a wide toe box. Many describe a painful break-in, often at the big toe, before it stretches to a good fit. Some find the heel baggy, and a few say the rubber wears faster than stiffer Instincts. Suits wide feet best.

Most reviewers like the Mega Jul for single-pitch lead and top-rope belaying: light, simple and durable, with little wear after years. The common complaint is friction and effort in guide mode and jerky, tiring rappels in assisted mode. Some find it fussy with certain ropes. Better suited to sport and gym than multipitch.

Most reviewers love the Drago for its soft, sensitive feel, sticky rubber and comfort once broken in, especially for indoor bouldering and smearing. The main downside is durability, with holes at the toes often appearing within a few months. Some also find it painful on long sessions. Best for short, powerful climbing rather than tiny edges.

Most reviewers find the Veloce very comfortable, soft and sticky, a favourite for gym and easy days, especially on wide feet. Downsides are that it wears out quickly, often needing a resole within months, and that many find the heel baggy. It is soft for tiny edges and technical climbing.

Reviewers praise the Drago LV for soft, sensitive feel and a snug, narrow heel that suits low-volume feet. Many report a painful break-in, and some wear through the soles within months. A few find the heel still baggy. Mainly suits bouldering and smearing, with less support on small edges.

Many reviewers swear by the TC Pro for trad, cracks and long multipitch days, finding it comfortable once broken in and durable. A large group, though, get pain from it, mostly at the heel, Achilles, tongue or arches. Fit is hit or miss, and it suits narrower feet better.

Most reviewers find the Kubo comfortable once broken in, a good step up from beginner shoes for gym and general climbing. Many report a painful first few sessions, and it stretches noticeably, so sizing down is common. A few find the heel too roomy for heel hooks.

Most reviewers with narrow or shallow heels find the Instinct VSR LV a great fit, with a snug heel for hooking and good comfort for a performance shoe. Some have a tough break-in, and a few find the toes painful. Best for low-volume heels.

Most reviewers find the Gomi comfortable and sticky, with a secure heel and good heel and toe hooks, and it suits wide forefeet with narrow heels well. Downsides are sizing, since toes can feel cramped or painful, and a few report the rubber wearing out fast. It is soft and not ideal for edging.

Opinions on the Giga Jul are split, though many like its versatility, covering assisted braking, guide mode and rappels in one device. Common complaints are friction when feeding or taking rope, especially with thick ropes, and locking that varies with the rope and carabiner. Some find rappelling and mode switching fiddly. Best as an all-rounder for those who accept the compromises.

Most reviewers see the Vapor V as a comfortable, moderately stiff all-rounder that holds up well. Common downsides are toe pain and a rough break-in for some, and a baggy heel that slips on hooks. Better for general gym and easy trad than for sensitivity.

Most reviewers love how smoothly the NEOX pays out rope for lead belaying, often compared favourably to a GRIGRI and feeling close to a tube device. Downsides are that catches can be softer with more rope paying out, it can lock up on thick ropes, and it is less suited to top rope or multipitch. A few dislike the clicking wheel.

Reviewers value the Instinct VS as a stiff, precise edging shoe that becomes comfortable and lasts well once broken in. Break-in is often painful, especially at the big toe knuckle, and several find the heel baggy. Suits wide feet and technical climbing more than soft smearing.

Most reviewers like the Drago XT for its soft, sensitive feel and secure heel that works for small heels, with a comfortable fit after break-in. Downsides include painful toes early on, a baggy heel for some, and worries about thin rubber wearing out. Break-in can take around ten sessions.

Most reviewers see the Helix as a comfortable, neutral, lace-up beginner shoe that is good value and lasts well, including for multipitch. It stretches, so buying snug is suggested, and a few find it limited on tiny holds and steep climbing. Suits first shoes and long easy days.

Reviewers like the Instinct S slipper for its secure heel, sensitivity and edging, especially with small or shallow heels. Toe pain is the common drawback, along with a tough break-in, and some found the toe box uncomfortable. Fit is hit or miss.

Most reviewers love the ATC-Pilot for smooth feeding and lowering, with a tube-like feel that is easy to switch to from an ATC, and good value. A few note slippage with some ropes or lighter belayers with heavy partners, and a plastic, hollow feel. Works best for single-pitch and gym.

Most reviewers find the Mandala comfortable and sensitive, with a snug heel and a durable build. It is stiffer than other soft shoes, and the no-edge design takes some getting used to. A few report toe or Achilles pain.

Most reviewers find the Indalo comfortable for a performance shoe, with good edging and toe hooks. Sizing is a recurring theme, as many go well below street size, and some feel toe pain or heel air pockets. Suits narrow heels.

Most reviewers use it to belay a much heavier climber and find it smoother and softer than the Ohm, with easier rope pulling for clips. Some had trouble with the weight-setting interface and the short sling on higher settings. A few reported it not camming on low falls, and one a damaged sling.

Most reviewers find it very comfortable, especially people with a small waist and big thighs or hips, thanks to adjustable leg loops and good padding. Its gear loops suit sport better than trad. A few found it bulky, tight at the legs, or limited in adjustment, and the smallest size has tiny loops.

Most reviewers find it very comfortable, with wide leg loops that are easy to forget about, and many use it in the gym or for sport and easy trad. The fixed leg loops need careful sizing, and people with large thighs and a smaller waist often struggle to get a good fit.

Most reviewers find it comfortable and long-lasting, and it is a popular first or second pair that suits wide and Egyptian-shaped feet. Heel fit is mixed, with a few finding it baggy or blistering while others with narrow heels find it fits well. A few report stretching or toe pain.

A very stiff, powerful shoe that many reviewers like for overhangs, boards and bouldering, with a heel that fits many feet well and decent lifespan. Most say it feels painful or hard when new and takes a few weeks to break in. Lighter climbers and those wanting feel find it too stiff.

Most reviewers find it very comfortable, especially people with wide feet or a low-volume heel, and some say it is the only shoe that fits them. It is stiff enough for edging yet sensitive. A few find the toes tight, and some wish it lasted longer.

Most reviewers praise its heel fit, especially for shallow or narrow heels, and it works well for heel and toe hooks. The main downside is that it wears out fast, with several reporting holes or worn rubber within a few months. A few call it expensive.

A comfortable, durable all-rounder that many reviewers use as a first shoe or gym workhorse, and it resoles well. Sized too aggressively it can hurt, and it needs a few sessions to break in. A few mention it stretching.

Large, stiff and very durable, with many reviewers using theirs for years and trusting it for solo bouldering. The main downsides are weight and bulk, which make it awkward to carry on long approaches and to fit in a car. A couple report the corners or velcro failing.

Reviewers split. Some like it for teaching beginners and for its anti-panic safety, while many dislike the lowering, which can be stop-start and fussy, especially on thick ropes or with lighter climbers. Paying out slack and the mode button also annoyed some. The steel plates seem to wear well.

A comfortable, affordable beginner shoe that many reviewers used for their first years or gym laps. Fit and wear are the drawbacks: several found the heel baggy or slipping, and a number wore holes or lost rubber within a few months. Not suited to harder or heel and toe climbing.

A stiffer, boxier shoe that some reviewers rate among their favourites once broken in. Sizing is the recurring issue: it runs small, many sized up, and it can feel painful at the toes or heel at first. Fit is hit or miss on narrow or low-volume feet.

A snug aggressive shoe with sticky rubber and a good toe patch, which many reviewers find comfortable and a strong gym all-rounder. Heel fit is a common issue, with dead space or slipping, and the midsole feels stiff to some. A few found it painful or wearing out quickly.

Several reviewers find it comfortable and a good-value gym and sport harness. Fit is the main problem for people with thick thighs or a small waist, where the leg loops pinch or fold. A few reported the plastic leg-loop buckles breaking.

A very comfortable, lightly downturned shoe that reviewers like as a first shoe, step-up shoe or all-day shoe, and it lasts reasonably well. It is soft, so it is less suited to micro edges or very hard climbing, and a few mention the heel or straps loosening.

Used to belay a much heavier climber, and many reviewers say it helps a lot by keeping the belayer from being yanked up. The trade-off is hard catches and short-roping when clipping, which several disliked enough to prefer or recommend the Ohmega.

A stiff, precise shoe that reviewers like for edging, trad and long multi-pitch, and its heel suits narrow feet. It can hurt at first, with toe and heel pain and break-in struggles. A few found it stiff for steep climbing and toe hooks, and sizing differs between versions.

Reviewers describe the Scarpa Booster as a soft, sensitive shoe with precise toes that sits between the Drago and the Instinct. The heel is the recurring catch: several find it baggy or dead-spaced, and one dislikes it, though a few like it for heel hooks. Very asymmetric, so it can tire flat feet.

The Scarpa Chimera is a lace-up, soft-feeling shoe that most reviewers rate as an excellent fit, especially for wide forefeet, with confident heel and toe hooking. The main downside is the heel, which several find baggy or too wide for narrow or low-volume feet. A few mention the laces or sizing running large.

Most reviewers find the Mad Rock D2.ONE HV very comfortable, snug and quick to break in, with a heel that hugs shallow or wide feet well. It is on the softer side and good for smearing, with some edging power. One reviewer found it insensitive and imprecise.

The Mad Rock Drone 2 LV is a snug, stiff shoe that suits narrow feet and shallow heels well, and many reviewers call it the best-fitting shoe they have worn once on. Downsides are that it is hard to get on, stiff and less sensitive for smearing, and it can loosen over time. Some found it too cramped.

The Evolv Phantom Pro is stiff in the toe for small chips on steep ground, with sticky rubber, a softer midfoot and a fit many find comfortable. The main downside is wear: some report the rubber wearing quickly, though one got months of daily use. Fit is not for everyone, with one painful return.

The Misty Mountain Cadillac is a plush, very comfortable trad and big wall harness with plenty of gear loops, double buckles and a durable build. Reviewers say it is heavy. One found it pinched the hips and had floppy gear loops, and another had buckles slowly loosen on walls.

The Scarpa Furia Air is a very soft shoe that reviewers love for sensitivity on smears and steep or friction rock. Downsides are a soft, baggy or stretchy heel, weak edging and hooking, and wear that many find quick. Best seen as a specialist soft shoe.

The Scarpa Generator Mid is a high-top crack and all-day shoe that most reviewers find comfortable, with good edging and foot jams, and less clunky than the TC Pro. It is fairly stiff and can feel heavy or hot. Fit is the catch: some found the heel loose or the shoe tight until it stretched.

The Black Diamond Method S is a fairly soft synthetic bouldering shoe that reviewers like for smearing, friction and a deep heel, and many find it durable. The common downside is a tight, painful break-in that can take a while, with little stretch. A few reported poor grip, cheap stitching or delamination.

The Black Diamond Aspect Pro is a comfortable crack and multipitch shoe that most reviewers prefer to the TC Pro for fit, with a good lace system and supportive feel for all-day climbing. Some praise the sticky rubber while one finds it less sticky. Delamination was reported by a couple of reviewers.

The Mad Rock Drone CS LV suits very narrow feet, and most reviewers love its slim, shallow heel and comfort once broken in. The main downside is a narrow toe box that crushes toes for some, along with a stiff, insensitive feel. A few say it never breaks in.

The La Sportiva Otaki is a stiff, comfortable all-rounder that reviewers like for standing on tiny holds, and it works well for wide midfeet and narrow heels. Heel and toe hooking are not its strength, and it is less precise than some stiffer shoes. Heavy downsizing hurts at first.

The Scarpa Arpia V is mostly praised as very comfortable, a solid all-rounder with good smearing. The main downsides are fast rubber wear for some, a loose or insecure heel for a few, and toe or heel pain for others until broken in. Little high rubber limits steep use.

The Mad Rock Remora Pro HV is a soft, sensitive shoe that reviewers like for smearing, with a snug heel that is tighter than the Drago and sticky rubber. It is strong in the gym and decent on small edges. It fits tighter than some expect, and one reviewer got intense heel pain.

The Evolv Phantom LV is aggressive and stiff, and reviewers mostly love it for very narrow, shallow heels and a precise outdoor performance. Break-in is the main downside, painful for some, and it is less versatile, working best on steep outdoor boulders. A couple found the heel baggy.

The Edelrid Autana is a comfortable harness that reviewers with large thighs praise most, thanks to its adjustable leg loops and thick padding that does not dig in. The waist belt stays centred. The main downside is the gear loops, which two reviewers found tiny or overlapped on smaller sizes.

The Evolv Geshido is a fairly stiff, supportive shoe that reviewers like for edging and long sport sessions, and it suits wider feet. It runs small and can be very tight at first, and one found it painful. Heel and toe hooking are weak.

Most reviewers find the Evolv Shaman Pro a snug, comfortable fit with a deep heel, good for toe hooks and steep gym climbing, and several with wide feet like it. The main complaint is tightness: a few who sized at street size found it painful, and some find it stiff, tricky to get into and fiddly at the closure.

Reviewers describe the Evolv Shaman 2S as a comfortable, softer and sensitive shoe with sticky rubber, a secure heel and little break-in. It suits board and gym climbing well. The main downside is softness: a few find it too soft, feeling it softens further during a session or struggles to dig into small holds.

Most reviewers find the La Sportiva Skwama Lite very comfortable, with a good heel fit and a slipper-like feel that softens after break-in. It also stretches noticeably. The rubber is the recurring letdown, with a few finding it less sticky, especially on small wood holds, and one resoled for better grip.

Reviewers like the Unparallel TN Pro as a fairly stiff, supportive all-rounder that smears well and works for board and gym climbing, softening and becoming more sensitive with time. It suits medium to wide feet well. The most repeated complaint is a baggy heel, and a few note the toe rand wearing at the toe when pivoting.

Most reviewers like the Scarpa Vapor S as a comfortable, do-it-all slipper with a notably snug heel, soft enough to smear yet precise on edges. The main downside is toe pain, with a few finding it crushing. Some with very shallow heels still have fit issues, and one found the closure fragile.

Most reviewers love the Scarpa Instinct, mainly the lace-up version, as a comfortable, supportive all-round shoe that is precise on edges and holds up over long routes. The main downside is a tough break-in with toe pain, which some solved by sizing up. A few saw the rubber wear quickly on sharp rock.

Reviewers are very happy with the Organic Full Pad, praising its dense, well-built foam, sturdy straps and long life. It is easy to carry and fits small cars. Some use two together or pair it with a bigger pad, as it gives less confidence on highballs. A few note it is heavier than similar pads.

Most reviewers find the Petzl CORAX comfortable and very adjustable, with two waist buckles that suit pear shapes and big hips or thighs, and it works well as a gym harness. The main downside is that some find it uncomfortable when hanging or sitting, and leg loops can run small or lack adjustment.

Most reviewers find the La Sportiva Tarantulace a comfortable, non-aggressive shoe that suits wide feet and all-day wear, and many climbed hard grades in it. The main downside is durability: some wore through the toes within a year or two, and a few say it edges and jams less well than the TC Pro.

Reviewers are split on the Tenaya Oasi. Fans praise a narrow, secure heel, easy toe hooks and comfort, and it suits narrow feet and heels. The main complaints are that it wears out quickly and stretches, and some find the rubber slippery or the fit baggy, too narrow or poor for wide feet.

Most reviewers love the Tenaya Oasi LV, mainly for a small, secure heel that suits shallow and narrow feet, and many call it comfortable and long-lasting, with several resoles. Narrow feet do best. The few downsides are a tight forefoot and, for one reviewer, Achilles pressure.

Most reviewers find the Edelrid Pinch smooth to belay with, similar to or a bit better than a GRIGRI, and like how it clips straight to the belay loop. It works best on thinner ropes. Downsides are draggy feeding on thick gym ropes, awkward racking and some sensitivity when lowering. A few see little gain over a GRIGRI.

Most reviewers find the Mad Rock Rover very comfortable and good value, with sticky rubber, suiting wide feet and beginners. It smears well but is soft for edging. The main downside is durability: several wore holes in the toes within months, though others report long life. Sizing too big stretches it out.

Most reviewers love the Scarpa Veloce L, a comfortable lace-up with very sticky rubber that smears well and suits wide feet and indoor or warm-up use. The recurring downside is a heel that bags out or is roomy over time, so several advise sizing down. It is less suited to hard heel or toe hooking.

Reviewers praise the heel of the Mad Rock Drone 2 HV as secure and the shoe as a comfortably tight fit once broken in. It is stiff and hard to get on at first, especially with high insteps. The main downside is durability, with several reporting torn rubber or holes within months.

Reviewers who like the Mad Rock RedLine Strap call it soft and sensitive with a good out-of-box fit, and some have worn it for years as an all-rounder. The main downside is a narrow fit that crushes toes, especially with wider feet. A few say it feels less comfortable and is poor for edging.

Reviewers find the Unparallel UP Mocc a comfortable, soft slipper with sticky rubber that suits wide and narrow feet, thin cracks, slabs and all-day wear. The downsides are limited support and weak edging, and one notes it is not good for heel hooks. It works as a comfort or trad shoe.
